201.event_title: Andrei Sakharov turns against nuclear testing
201.event: Andrei Sakharov, a physicist who had played a leading part in building the Soviet hydrogen bomb, became concerned in 1957 about the biological hazards of radioactive fallout from nuclear tests and began campaigning to halt or limit testing, which brought him into conflict with Nikita Khrushchev in 1961. He later said he had helped promote the 1963 treaty banning nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in outer space and under water. After a 1968 essay of his was published abroad he was removed from weapons work, and in 1975 he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, which the Soviet authorities did not allow him to travel to Oslo to receive.
201.explanation: One of the people best placed to understand the harm his work could do was the one who grew most alarmed by it, at real cost to his own career and safety.
201.tie_back: The kural says that the noble dread evil deeds while hardened wrongdoers feel no fear, and Sakharov's growing dread of the harm his weapons could cause marked him out among those around him.
201._accuracy_note: A strong picture of moral dread as a sign of excellence, though the kural's contrast with desensitised wrongdoers is implied rather than shown.

202.event_title: The Watergate cover-up brings down President Nixon
202.event: After men connected to President Richard Nixon's re-election committee were caught breaking into the Democratic National Committee offices in the Watergate complex in June 1972, Nixon and his aides worked to hide the White House's links to the break-in. A recording of 23 June 1972 captured Nixon approving a plan to have the CIA ask the FBI to halt its investigation. When the Supreme Court ordered the tapes released, this conversation became public in August 1974, his remaining support collapsed, and he resigned on 9 August 1974, the only US president to do so.
202.explanation: Watergate is the classic example of a cover-up doing more damage than the original wrongdoing, as each new concealment created new offences.
202.tie_back: The kural says evil must be feared more than fire because it gives birth to further evil, and the Watergate break-in led step by step to obstruction of justice and the downfall of a presidency.
202._accuracy_note: A very clear real-world case of one wrong breeding further wrongs that ended up consuming the wrongdoer.

203.event_title: Herbert Hoover's American Relief Administration feeds famine-stricken Soviet Russia
203.event: In 1921, after the writer Maxim Gorky appealed abroad for help with a severe famine in Soviet Russia, Herbert Hoover, head of the American Relief Administration, negotiated an agreement to organise relief inside the country, even though the United States and the Soviet government were deeply hostile to each other. Funded by voluntary contributions and a 20 million dollar appropriation from the US Congress, the ARA's kitchens were feeding nearly 11 million people a day by the summer of 1922, and it also supplied medicine to thousands of hospitals. Historians still debate the mission's politics, but its scale is well documented.
203.explanation: A country that regarded the Soviet regime as an enemy nevertheless fed millions of its people in their time of need.
203.tie_back: The kural calls it the highest wisdom to refrain from doing harm even to those who are hostile to us, and the ARA went further, doing large-scale good in a country whose government the United States opposed.
203._accuracy_note: The hostility here was between governments rather than a personal enemy who had harmed the giver, so the fit with non-retaliation is partial.

204.event_title: Titus Oates and the invented Popish Plot
204.event: In 1678 Titus Oates, a former Anglican clergyman, swore to a fictitious Jesuit plot to assassinate King Charles II and put his Catholic brother James, Duke of York, on the throne. In the panic that followed, about 35 innocent people were put to death on the strength of the accusations before inconsistencies in his story came to light. In 1684 the Duke of York won 100,000 pounds in damages from Oates for libel, and after James became king in 1685 Oates was convicted of perjury and severely punished, including the pillory and imprisonment.
204.explanation: The man who manufactured a plot to destroy others was eventually ruined by the exposure of his own lies.
204.tie_back: The kural warns that whoever plots another's ruin will find virtue itself plotting his ruin in turn, and Oates's invented conspiracy ended in his own conviction and disgrace.
204._accuracy_note: A close match to the plot that recoils on the plotter, although Oates was released and pensioned after 1688, so the recoil was not total.

205.event_title: Nick Leeson's hidden losses break Barings Bank
205.event: Nick Leeson, a trader for Britain's Barings Bank in Singapore, used a secret error account numbered 88888 to hide his trading losses, which had reached hundreds of millions of Singapore dollars by December 1994. After the Kobe earthquake in January 1995 sent the Tokyo market sharply lower, he kept making larger bets in an attempt to recover, and he fled Singapore on 23 February 1995, after which auditors found losses of about 2.2 billion Singapore dollars. Barings, one of Britain's oldest merchant banks, collapsed and was sold to the Dutch group ING for a token one pound, and Leeson was sentenced in Singapore to six and a half years in prison.
205.explanation: Each attempt to escape a hole by concealment and further risk made the hole deeper, until it swallowed the bank.
205.tie_back: The kural warns that evil done to escape want only makes a person poorer still, and Leeson's hidden trades, made to recover losses, turned a loss into the ruin of the whole bank and of himself.
205._accuracy_note: The cycle of wrongdoing to escape a shortfall fits well, though Leeson was escaping trading losses rather than personal poverty.

206.event: Maximilien Robespierre was the dominant figure on the Committee of Public Safety during the Reign of Terror of 1793-1794, when many thousands of people were executed as enemies of the Revolution. As opposition to the Terror grew, the National Convention ordered his arrest on 9 Thermidor (27 July 1794). The next day he and 21 of his followers were executed by guillotine at the Place de la Revolution, and his fall opened the Thermidorian Reaction against the Terror.
206.explanation: The leader most identified with sending others to the scaffold was himself sent there by the same revolutionary machinery.
206.tie_back: The kural says that whoever does not want suffering should never inflict it on others, and Robespierre met the very fate the Terror had dealt out to so many.
206._accuracy_note: A strong historical case of harm returning to the one who inflicted it, though the kural speaks of a general moral law rather than political reversal.

207.event_title: Adolf Eichmann is found in Argentina and brought to trial
207.event: Adolf Eichmann, the SS officer who had organised the deportation of Jews to the Nazi camps, escaped justice after the Second World War and was living in Argentina under the name Ricardo Klement. Israeli agents seized him near his home in Buenos Aires on 11 May 1960 and flew him to Israel. His trial in Jerusalem began on 11 April 1961, he was found guilty on all counts in December 1961, and he was executed in 1962.
207.explanation: Fifteen years of hiding on another continent did not end the consequences of what Eichmann had done.
207.tie_back: The kural says people may escape any human enmity, but the enmity of their own evil deeds never dies and follows them to destroy them, and Eichmann's past pursued him across the world.
207._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of deeds that pursue the doer, though the pursuit here was carried out by human agents acting on those deeds.

208.event: In April 1983 the West German magazine Stern announced that it had obtained Adolf Hitler's secret diaries, for which it had paid 9.3 million marks through its reporter Gerd Heidemann. Within weeks the West German Federal Archives established that the notebooks had been produced after the war; they had been forged by Konrad Kujau, and Heidemann had kept millions of marks of the payments for himself. In 1985 a Hamburg court sentenced both men to more than four years in prison.
208.explanation: A forgery and a fraud that promised fortune and fame brought prison and lasting disgrace on the men who carried them out.
208.tie_back: The kural compares ruin to a shadow that never leaves the evildoer's feet, and the forgery and fraud brought both men a disgrace that stayed with them for the rest of their lives.
208._accuracy_note: Ruin did follow the wrongdoers, but the shadow image of lifelong, inseparable consequence is only partly shown by a single fraud and its punishment.

209.event_title: Hansie Cronje is banned from cricket for life
209.event: Hansie Cronje, the widely admired captain of South Africa's cricket team, initially denied allegations made by New Delhi police in April 2000 that he had taken money from a bookmaker, but then admitted wrongdoing and lost the captaincy. In June 2000 he told the government-appointed King Commission that he had received thousands of dollars from gamblers and bookmakers on five separate occasions between 1996 and 2000, and that he had offered teammates money to underperform. In October 2000 the United Cricket Board of South Africa banned him for life from all its cricket activities.
209.explanation: Payments that may have seemed small and private ended a celebrated career and turned a national hero into a byword for corruption in sport.
209.tie_back: The kural says that anyone who truly loves himself will not go near even the smallest evil, and Cronje's acceptance of bookmakers' money destroyed everything he had built for himself.
209._accuracy_note: A strong case of a small-seeming wrong destroying the wrongdoer's own good, which is exactly the self-interest argument of the kural.

210.event_title: Lal Bahadur Shastri resigns as Railways Minister
210.event: Lal Bahadur Shastri, India's Minister for Railways, resigned in 1956 after a major railway accident in Madras state (at Ariyalur) caused heavy loss of life, taking responsibility although he was not personally at fault. His biographer in the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography calls this a demonstration, rare in post-independence Indian politics, of strict responsibility and accountability. He was brought back into the government in 1957, became Home Minister in 1961, and was chosen as India's second Prime Minister on 9 June 1964.
210.explanation: Shastri's refusal to evade responsibility, and his reputation for simple, honest living, did not end his career but became the foundation of the trust that later made him Prime Minister.
210.tie_back: The kural assures that one who never swerves from the right path is safe from ruin, and Shastri's resignation, far from ruining him, raised him in public esteem.
210._accuracy_note: It shows integrity followed by lasting standing, but a single resignation cannot fully demonstrate a lifetime of never straying from the path.
